Z-Residual Diagnostic Tool for Assessing Covariate Functional Form

Tingxuan Wu

2026-07-30

Source: vignettes/articles/demo_zresid_frailty_model.qmd

Introduction

This vignette explains how to use the Zresidual package to calculate Z-residuals from models fitted with coxph() in the survival package. It also demonstrates how Z-residuals can assess overall goodness of fit (GOF) and identify specific model misspecifications in semiparametric shared-frailty models.

For detailed definitions and the complete data analysis, refer to the paper Z-residual diagnostics for detecting misspecification of the functional form of covariates for shared frailty models.

Definition of Z-residual

We use Z-residuals to diagnose shared-frailty models in a Cox proportional hazards setting with an unspecified baseline hazard. Suppose there are g groups of individuals, with group i containing n_i individuals, i = 1,\ldots,g. Let y_{ij} be a possibly right-censored observation for the jth individual in group i, and let \delta_{ij} indicate whether the observation is uncensored.

The randomized survival probability (RSP) for y_{ij} is

S_{ij}^{R}(y_{ij}, \delta_{ij}, U_{ij}) = \begin{cases} S_{ij}(y_{ij}), & \text{if } \delta_{ij}=1,\\ U_{ij}S_{ij}(y_{ij}), & \text{if } \delta_{ij}=0, \end{cases}

where U_{ij} is a uniform random variable on (0,1) and S_{ij}(\cdot) is the postulated survival function given the covariates x_{ij}. When y_{ij} is censored, S_{ij}^{R} is randomized between 0 and S_{ij}(y_{ij}).

Under the true model, the RSPs are uniformly distributed on (0,1) given x_i. They can therefore be transformed into residuals with a desired reference distribution. We use the standard normal quantile:

r_{ij}^{Z}(y_{ij}, \delta_{ij}, U_{ij}) = -\Phi^{-1}\left\{ S_{ij}^{R}(y_{ij}, \delta_{ij}, U_{ij}) \right\}.

Under the true model, these residuals follow a standard normal distribution. Consequently, diagnostic methods developed for normal regression can also be used with censored data. The normal transformation also makes extremely small or large RSPs easier to identify; even a small number of such extreme values may indicate model misspecification.

Installation

You can install the development version of Zresidual from GitHub:

Code
if (!requireNamespace("Zresidual", quietly = TRUE)) {
  if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("remotes")
  remotes::install_github("tiw150/Zresidual", upgrade = "never", dependencies = TRUE)
}

Load the packages used in this vignette:

Code
library(Zresidual)
library(survival)

The optional DT and gifski packages are used for interactive tables and animated diagnostic figures, respectively.

Examples for Illustration and Demonstration

A real dataset

This example illustrates how Z-residuals diagnose both overall GOF and the functional form of covariates in an analysis of survival times for patients with acute myeloid leukemia.

The dataset contains 411 patients recorded at the M. D. Anderson Cancer Center between 1980 and 1996. The patients were under age 60 and came from 24 administrative districts. The available prognostic factors include age, sex, white blood cell count (wbc) at diagnosis, and the Townsend score (tpi), where higher values indicate less affluent areas. The censoring rate is 29.2%. The response is survival time in days from study entry to death or censoring.

Preliminary analysis showed that wbc is highly right-skewed. A logarithmic transformation is often used to reduce the influence of extremely large covariate values, but it may also mask their relationship with the outcome.

leuksurv_path <- system.file(
  "extdata",
  "LeukSurv.rda",
  package = "Zresidual"
)

if (nzchar(leuksurv_path)) {
  load(leuksurv_path)
} else {
  # Compatibility with package versions that exposed the dataset through data().
  data("LeukSurv", package = "Zresidual", envir = environment())
}

if (!exists("LeukSurv")) {
  stop("The LeukSurv dataset could not be loaded.", call. = FALSE)
}

LeukSurv$district <- as.factor(LeukSurv$district)
LeukSurv$sex <- as.factor(LeukSurv$sex)
LeukSurv$logwbc <- log(LeukSurv$wbc + 0.001)
LeukSurv <- droplevels(LeukSurv[LeukSurv$age < 60, ])
Code
if (requireNamespace("DT", quietly = TRUE)) {
  DT::datatable(
    LeukSurv,
    caption = "Table 1: Acute myeloid leukemia survival data.",
    options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)
  )
} else {
  knitr::kable(
    head(LeukSurv, 20),
    caption = "Table 1: Acute myeloid leukemia survival data (first 20 rows)."
  )
}

Fit the models

We fit two shared-frailty models. The wbc model includes untransformed wbc, age, sex, and tpi. The lwbc model replaces wbc with log(wbc).

fit_LeukSurv_wbc <- coxph(
  Surv(time, cens) ~ age + sex + wbc + tpi +
    frailty(district, distribution = "gamma"),
  data = LeukSurv
)

fit_LeukSurv_logwbc <- coxph(
  Surv(time, cens) ~ age + sex + logwbc + tpi +
    frailty(district, distribution = "gamma"),
  data = LeukSurv
)

Z-residual calculation

Once the models have been fitted, calculate 1,000 randomized Z-residual replicates and extract the aligned covariate information used by the plotting and testing functions.

Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc <- Zresidual(
  fit = fit_LeukSurv_wbc,
  data = LeukSurv,
  nrep = nrep,
  seed = 123
)

Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc <- Zresidual(
  fit = fit_LeukSurv_logwbc,
  data = LeukSurv,
  nrep = nrep,
  seed = 456
)

zcov.LeukSurv.wbc <- Zcov(fit_LeukSurv_wbc, data = LeukSurv)
zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc <- Zcov(fit_LeukSurv_logwbc, data = LeukSurv)

Graphically assess the models

Overall goodness of fit

A normal Q-Q plot of the Z-residuals provides a graphical assessment of overall GOF. The Shapiro-Wilk (SW) and Shapiro-Francia (SF) normality tests provide numerical assessments. For these data, the Q-Q plots for both models align reasonably well with the 45-degree reference line, and the Z-SW tests generally give large p-values.

wbc model code
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  qqnorm(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.wbc,
    irep = i,
    main.title = "Z-residual Q-Q plot: wbc model"
  )
}
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  qqnorm(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    irep = i,
    main.title = "Z-residual Q-Q plot: lwbc model"
  )
}

The Z-residuals can also be grouped by intervals of the linear predictor or a covariate. We can then assess whether the grouped residuals have homogeneous distributions. ANOVA F-tests compare group means, and Bartlett tests compare group variances.

For both models, the scatterplots of Z-residuals against the linear predictor show no prominent trend: the LOWESS curves remain close to zero. The grouped boxplots also suggest similar means and variances. Correspondingly, Z-AOV-LP and Z-BL-LP generally produce large p-values.

wbc scatterplot code
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  plot(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.wbc,
    x_axis_var = "lp",
    irep = i,
    add_lowess = TRUE,
    main.title = "Scatterplot: wbc model"
  )
}
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  plot(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    x_axis_var = "lp",
    irep = i,
    add_lowess = TRUE,
    main.title = "Scatterplot: lwbc model"
  )
}
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  boxplot(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.wbc,
    x_axis_var = "lp",
    irep = i,
    main.title = "Boxplot: wbc model"
  )
}
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  boxplot(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    x_axis_var = "lp",
    irep = i,
    main.title = "Boxplot: lwbc model"
  )
}

Identifying a misspecified covariate functional form

The overall diagnostics do not reveal serious misspecification in either model. Diagnostics against wbc and logwbc, however, suggest that the functional form in the lwbc model is misspecified.

For the wbc model, the LOWESS curve remains close to zero and the grouped Z-residuals have similar means and variances. For the lwbc model, the LOWESS curve shows a nonlinear trend and the grouped residuals have different means. The very small Z-AOV-log(wbc) p-values provide strong evidence that the log transformation is inappropriate for modelling survival time in this example.

wbc model scatterplot code
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  plot(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.wbc,
    x_axis_var = "wbc",
    irep = i,
    add_lowess = TRUE,
    main.title = "Scatterplot: wbc model"
  )
}
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  plot(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    x_axis_var = "logwbc",
    irep = i,
    add_lowess = TRUE,
    main.title = "Scatterplot: lwbc model"
  )
}
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  boxplot(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.wbc,
    x_axis_var = "wbc",
    irep = i,
    main.title = "Boxplot: wbc model"
  )
}
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  boxplot(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    x_axis_var = "logwbc",
    irep = i,
    main.title = "Boxplot: lwbc model"
  )
}

The boxplots against the categorical covariate sex show similar means and variances across groups for both models. The corresponding Z-AOV and Z-BL p-values are generally greater than 0.05.

wbc model code
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  boxplot(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.wbc,
    x_axis_var = "sex",
    irep = i,
    main.title = "Boxplot: wbc model"
  )
}
for (i in 1:animation_reps) {
  boxplot(
    Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc,
    x_axis_var = "sex",
    irep = i,
    main.title = "Boxplot: lwbc model"
  )
}

Quantitatively assess the models

The Shapiro-Wilk and Shapiro-Francia tests assess the normality of each randomized Z-residual replicate and therefore the overall GOF. The Shapiro-Francia test can also be extended to censored Z-residuals through gof.censored.zresidual().

sw.wbc <- sw.test.zresid(Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc)
sw.lwbc <- sw.test.zresid(Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc)
sf.wbc <- sf_test.zresid(Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc)
sf.lwbc <- sf_test.zresid(Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc)

gof_tests <- data.frame(
  replicate = seq_len(nrep),
  `Z-SW: wbc model` = sw.wbc,
  `Z-SW: lwbc model` = sw.lwbc,
  `Z-SF: wbc model` = sf.wbc,
  `Z-SF: lwbc model` = sf.lwbc,
  check.names = FALSE
)
Code
if (requireNamespace("DT", quietly = TRUE)) {
  DT::datatable(
    gof_tests,
    caption = paste(
      "Table 2: Replicated Z-SW and Z-SF p-values for the wbc",
      "and lwbc models."
    ),
    options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)
  )
} else {
  knitr::kable(
    head(gof_tests, 20),
    caption = paste(
      "Table 2: Replicated Z-SW and Z-SF p-values for the wbc",
      "and lwbc models (first 20 rows)."
    )
  )
}

The Z-residuals can be grouped by intervals of a covariate or linear predictor. ANOVA tests compare the group means, while Bartlett tests compare the group variances.

aov.wbc.lp <- aov.test.zresid(
  Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc,
  X = "lp",
  zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.wbc,
  k.anova = 10
)

aov.lwbc.lp <- aov.test.zresid(
  Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  X = "lp",
  zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  k.anova = 10
)

bl.wbc.lp <- bartlett.test.zresid(
  Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc,
  X = "lp",
  zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.wbc,
  k.bl = 10
)

bl.lwbc.lp <- bartlett.test.zresid(
  Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  X = "lp",
  zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  k.bl = 10
)

aov.wbc <- aov.test.zresid(
  Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc,
  X = "wbc",
  zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.wbc,
  k.anova = 10
)

aov.lwbc <- aov.test.zresid(
  Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  X = "logwbc",
  zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  k.anova = 10
)

bl.wbc <- bartlett.test.zresid(
  Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc,
  X = "wbc",
  zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.wbc,
  k.bl = 10
)

bl.lwbc <- bartlett.test.zresid(
  Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  X = "logwbc",
  zcov = zcov.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  k.bl = 10
)

homogeneity_tests <- data.frame(
  replicate = seq_len(nrep),
  `Z-AOV-LP: wbc model` = aov.wbc.lp,
  `Z-AOV-LP: lwbc model` = aov.lwbc.lp,
  `Z-BL-LP: wbc model` = bl.wbc.lp,
  `Z-BL-LP: lwbc model` = bl.lwbc.lp,
  `Z-AOV-wbc: wbc model` = aov.wbc,
  `Z-AOV-log(wbc): lwbc model` = aov.lwbc,
  `Z-BL-wbc: wbc model` = bl.wbc,
  `Z-BL-log(wbc): lwbc model` = bl.lwbc,
  check.names = FALSE
)
Code
if (requireNamespace("DT", quietly = TRUE)) {
  DT::datatable(
    homogeneity_tests,
    caption = paste(
      "Table 3: Replicated Z-AOV-LP, Z-AOV-covariate, Z-BL-LP,",
      "and Z-BL-covariate p-values for the wbc and lwbc models."
    ),
    options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)
  )
} else {
  knitr::kable(
    head(homogeneity_tests, 20),
    caption = paste(
      "Table 3: Replicated homogeneity-test p-values",
      "(first 20 rows)."
    )
  )
}

The following histograms display the 1,000 replicated p-values. The red vertical lines are the conservative upper-bound p-values obtained from the replicated results. Z-SW, Z-SF, and Z-AOV-LP produce substantial proportions of p-values above 0.05 for both models. In contrast, nearly all replicated Z-AOV-log(wbc) p-values for the lwbc model are below 0.001, reinforcing the evidence that the logarithmic transformation is inappropriate here.

Code
par(mfrow = c(4, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 2))

hist(
  sw.wbc,
  main = "Replicated Z-SW p-values: wbc model",
  breaks = 20,
  xlab = "p-value"
)
abline(v = upper_bound_pvalue(sw.wbc), col = "red", lwd = 2)

hist(
  sw.lwbc,
  main = "Replicated Z-SW p-values: lwbc model",
  breaks = 20,
  xlab = "p-value"
)
abline(v = upper_bound_pvalue(sw.lwbc), col = "red", lwd = 2)

hist(
  sf.wbc,
  main = "Replicated Z-SF p-values: wbc model",
  breaks = 20,
  xlab = "p-value"
)
abline(v = upper_bound_pvalue(sf.wbc), col = "red", lwd = 2)

hist(
  sf.lwbc,
  main = "Replicated Z-SF p-values: lwbc model",
  breaks = 20,
  xlab = "p-value"
)
abline(v = upper_bound_pvalue(sf.lwbc), col = "red", lwd = 2)

hist(
  aov.wbc.lp,
  main = "Replicated Z-AOV-LP p-values: wbc model",
  breaks = 20,
  xlab = "p-value"
)
abline(v = upper_bound_pvalue(aov.wbc.lp), col = "red", lwd = 2)

hist(
  aov.lwbc.lp,
  main = "Replicated Z-AOV-LP p-values: lwbc model",
  breaks = 20,
  xlab = "p-value"
)
abline(v = upper_bound_pvalue(aov.lwbc.lp), col = "red", lwd = 2)

hist(
  aov.wbc,
  main = "Replicated Z-AOV-wbc p-values: wbc model",
  breaks = 20,
  xlab = "p-value"
)
abline(v = upper_bound_pvalue(aov.wbc), col = "red", lwd = 2)

hist(

For direct comparison, the upper-bound p-values represented by the red vertical lines in the histograms are summarized below.

upper_bound_summary <- data.frame(
  Diagnostic = c(
    "Z-SW",
    "Z-SF",
    "Z-AOV-LP",
    "Z-AOV-covariate"
  ),
  `wbc model` = c(
    upper_bound_pvalue(sw.wbc),
    upper_bound_pvalue(sf.wbc),
    upper_bound_pvalue(aov.wbc.lp),
    upper_bound_pvalue(aov.wbc)
  ),
  `lwbc model` = c(
    upper_bound_pvalue(sw.lwbc),
    upper_bound_pvalue(sf.lwbc),
    upper_bound_pvalue(aov.lwbc.lp),
    upper_bound_pvalue(aov.lwbc)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  upper_bound_summary,
  digits = 6,
  align = c("l", "r", "r"),
  caption = paste(
    "Table 4: Conservative upper-bound p-values corresponding to",
    "the red vertical lines in the replicated p-value histograms."
  )
)

Other Residual Calculations

Censored Z-residuals

The normality of censored Z-residuals can be tested by an extended Shapiro-Francia method for censored observations, implemented by gof.censored.zresidual().

censored.Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc <- surv_residuals(
  fit.object = fit_LeukSurv_wbc,
  data = LeukSurv,
  residual.type = "censored Z-residual"
)

censored.Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc <- surv_residuals(
  fit.object = fit_LeukSurv_logwbc,
  data = LeukSurv,
  residual.type = "censored Z-residual"
)

gof.censored.zresidual(
  censored.Zresidual = censored.Zresid.LeukSurv.wbc
)
[1] 0.5495629
gof.censored.zresidual(
  censored.Zresidual = censored.Zresid.LeukSurv.logwbc
)
[1] 0.3387376

Cox-Snell residuals

The overall GOF tests and graphical checks based on Cox-Snell residuals suggest that both models fit the dataset adequately. For each model, the estimated cumulative hazard function of the Cox-Snell residuals lies close to the 45-degree reference line.

ucs.LeukSurv.wbc <- surv_residuals(
  fit.object = fit_LeukSurv_wbc,
  data = LeukSurv,
  residual.type = "Cox-Snell"
)

ucs.LeukSurv.logwbc <- surv_residuals(
  fit.object = fit_LeukSurv_logwbc,
  data = LeukSurv,
  residual.type = "Cox-Snell"
)

plot(
  ucs.LeukSurv.wbc,
  main.title = "Cox-Snell residuals: wbc model",
  outlier.return = FALSE
)

plot(
  ucs.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  main.title = "Cox-Snell residuals: lwbc model",
  outlier.return = FALSE
)

Martingale residuals

The martingale residuals are mostly in the interval (-3,1) for both models. For the wbc model, the LOWESS curve has a slight upward slope on the left. For the lwbc model, the curve has a more pronounced downward shape. Neither curve is completely horizontal.

martg.LeukSurv.wbc <- surv_residuals(
  fit.object = fit_LeukSurv_wbc,
  data = LeukSurv,
  residual.type = "martingale"
)

martg.LeukSurv.logwbc <- surv_residuals(
  fit.object = fit_LeukSurv_logwbc,
  data = LeukSurv,
  residual.type = "martingale"
)

plot(
  martg.LeukSurv.wbc,
  x_axis_var = "wbc",
  main.title = "Martingale residuals: wbc model",
  outlier.return = FALSE
)

plot(
  martg.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  x_axis_var = "logwbc",
  main.title = "Martingale residuals: lwbc model",
  outlier.return = FALSE
)

Deviance residuals

The deviance residuals are more symmetric than the martingale residuals and mostly lie in the interval (-3,3). In both models, the LOWESS curves show noticeably non-horizontal trends.

dev.LeukSurv.wbc <- surv_residuals(
  fit.object = fit_LeukSurv_wbc,
  data = LeukSurv,
  residual.type = "deviance"
)

dev.LeukSurv.logwbc <- surv_residuals(
  fit.object = fit_LeukSurv_logwbc,
  data = LeukSurv,
  residual.type = "deviance"
)

plot(
  dev.LeukSurv.wbc,
  x_axis_var = "wbc",
  main.title = "Deviance residuals: wbc model",
  outlier.return = FALSE
)

plot(
  dev.LeukSurv.logwbc,
  x_axis_var = "logwbc",
  main.title = "Deviance residuals: lwbc model",
  outlier.return = FALSE
)
